text: MongoDB caps a single document at 16 MiB. 10,000 user ids fit well under that, so the practical reasons to move tags to separate entries are the cost of rewriting and reading one ever-growing document and the need to paginate, rather than the hard limit.
why: Gives the real document-size limit so learners don't conclude 10,000 ids cannot fit in one document.

text: Arrays can be indexed: MongoDB creates a multikey index automatically on an array field, with one index entry per element, and PostgreSQL indexes arrays with GIN (built-in array_ops supports @> and &&). PostgreSQL's docs still advise that if you search for array elements, a separate table with a row per element is easier to search and scales better.
why: Corrects 'arrays are unindexable' while keeping the teacher's design conclusion.

text: Facebook's Graph API stores photo tag positions exactly this way: the x and y of a tag are floats giving the 'percentage offset from the left edge' and 'from the top edge' of the picture.
why: A real production API confirms the relative-position design.

text: Object-detection datasets use the second form: YOLO labels store each box as class x_center y_center width height, normalized to 0-1 by dividing x and width by the image width and y and height by the image height.
why: Shows a widely used normalized bounding-box convention the front end or ML team may already use.

text: On 2 November 2021 Meta shut down the Face Recognition system on Facebook and said it would delete more than a billion face templates; people can no longer turn on face recognition for suggested tagging.
why: Updates the 'as Facebook does' example; face-based tag suggestions also carry privacy and regulatory weight.

text: In role-based access control (NIST) permissions are attached to roles and users get them through role membership. A 'who can tag me' setting depends on the relationship between two users, which is how Google's Zanzibar ACL system models permissions for Drive, Photos and YouTube.
why: Gives the right name and model for the tagging-permission layer.

text: Amazon's Builders' Library argues against most fallbacks: fallback code is hard to test, often has latent bugs and can make outages worse. It prefers making the primary path more robust, failing fast, and using code paths that run in production all the time.
why: Balances 'add a fallback' with why fallbacks need to be simple and exercised.

text: Android supports clubbing notifications: related notifications can be put in one group with a summary (Android 7.0+), and the system auto-groups an app's notifications once it posts four or more. Android's docs also suggest updating an existing notification instead of posting new ones.
why: Shows the platform mechanism behind 'club them'.

text: PostgreSQL states the rule behind this choice: equality conditions on leading index columns plus an inequality on the first column without an equality limit the part of the index scanned. With to = ? AND ts > ?, an index on (to, ts, ...) reads only the recent entries; (to, from, ts) reads all of the recipient's entries.
why: Gives the general rule for ordering composite-index columns (equality first, then range).

text: In SQL the aggregate is COUNT(DISTINCT expr), which counts distinct non-NULL values. FROM and TO are reserved words in MySQL, so columns named that way must be quoted with backticks; names like sender_id/recipient_id avoid the problem.
why: Lets readers run the board query as written.

text: In Redis, SCARD returns the number of members of a set in O(1), and returns 0 if the key does not exist, so a cleared badge needs no special case.
why: Names the exact command and confirms the O(1) claim.

text: Redis SADD ignores members already in the set and returns how many new members were added, 0 for a repeat sender. So the write is idempotent, and the worker can tell whether the sender was new.
why: Explains why repeat messages don't change the set and what the worker gets back.

text: Redis DEL on a set is O(M) in the number of members (O(1) only for string values). UNLINK removes the key in O(1) and reclaims memory in a background thread. For small per-user sets either is cheap.
why: Corrects the O(1) delete claim and names the non-blocking alternative.

text: Redis can do the auxiliary 'check and set' in one atomic command: SET key value NX sets the key only if it does not exist and returns OK when it did (nil otherwise). Adding EX seconds gives the key a TTL, so stale entries eventually disappear.
why: Removes the race between two workers and bounds stale auxiliary keys.

text: An alternative to one key per (receiver, sender) pair is one hash per receiver: HSETNX B C 1 sets field C only if it is absent and returns 1 if it did. A single DEL B clears the user, and since Redis 7.4 HEXPIRE can give individual fields a TTL.
why: Makes the clear path a single delete instead of enumerating keys.

text: In a Redis Cluster, keys are spread across hash slots, so B_C and B_D can land on different nodes. A hash tag such as {B}_C and {B}_D hashes only the part in braces, so all of a user's keys share one slot and can be handled together.
why: Clustering the auxiliary store changes how per-user keys must be named.

text: Kafka writes events with the same key to the same partition, and a consumer reads a partition's events in the order they were written. Keying on-message-unsent events by recipient id therefore sends all of a recipient's events to one worker, which can collapse them before writing.
why: Explains why partitioning by recipient id enables batching.

text: Batched Redis writes can be sent with pipelining: many commands go out without waiting for each reply. That saves round trips and system calls, and Redis reports throughput rising up to about 10x the unpipelined baseline.
why: Gives the Redis-side mechanism for the batching the teacher mentions.

text: A WebSocket connection can look open after the client has gone (e.g. lost network). RFC 6455 Ping/Pong frames are the protocol's way to check: a Ping 'may serve either as a keepalive or as a means to verify that the remote endpoint is still responsive', and the peer must answer with a Pong.
why: Online/offline detection based on sockets needs heartbeats to be reliable.

text: Redis replication is asynchronous and is documented as usable 'for scalability, to have multiple replicas for read-only queries'. In Redis Cluster, clients send READONLY to read from replicas where possibly stale data is acceptable.
why: Shows the standard way to scale the badge read path if needed.

text: In MySQL, plain EXPLAIN shows the optimizer's plan without running the query, but EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the statement and reports real timings. On a production console, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE with care, especially on heavy queries.
why: Safety note for the advice to run EXPLAIN on production.

text: MongoDB gives set semantics on an array field: $addToSet adds a value only if it is not already present. Updates to a single document are atomic, so concurrent workers adding senders for the same user don't corrupt the set.
why: Shows the student's MongoDB option supports the same 'database does the set check' idea as Redis.
